rationale: A wins because it knows where the floor ends. Its refusal of "A customer-story angle" is exactly the discipline this assignment needed, while B dresses that same missing proof up as "The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code." B has more angles, but one of them is a loaded mousetrap: no customer, no production-code proof, no procurement evidence, and still presented as viable.
gaps_in_A: "Figma's first big swing since the Adobe deal died" overstates the facts. The update says the launch follows the Adobe deal collapse; it does not say this is Figma's first major move since then.

The Adobe-aftermath angle needs a sharper outlet split. "Enterprise-software business reporter" is good, but this may also belong to M&A/antitrust aftermath reporters, not just software-industry trades.
The AI assistant is mostly swallowed by the codegen angle. If prompt-to-layout has a separate proof point, A doesn't try to find it; if it doesn't, that refusal should be explicit.
gaps_in_B: "The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code" invents the dangerous part. The facts say working front-end code, not production code, shipped code, approved code, or code entering enterprise repos.

"Design-to-code has been promised for a decade and has repeatedly produced unmaintainable output" may be true, but it is not in the provided update. In this exercise, unsupported category lore is still unsupported.
"a year of distance may have cooled it" is a sloppy outside-time claim. The update gives no collapse date, and the line weakens an otherwise legitimate Adobe-aftershock angle.

The recommended next step, "newsjack-detector," is cute but misdirected. This is a company launch with three pitchable beats; the next move is proof gathering plus journalist-fit-check, not hunting for a second peg.
